claims.text: As-synthesized HfNbTiVAl10 exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure with well-defined phase boundaries and grain networks.
High-speed DIC can capture real-time strain localization during tensile and fracture testing of HfNbTiVAl10.
High-speed DIC can capture crack propagation during testing of HfNbTiVAl10.
Post-test cryo-TEM or SEM can identify localized microstructural features relevant to deformation and fracture.
Evolving local strain fields correlate with phase boundaries, grain clusters, and interface characteristics in the hierarchical heterostructure.
DIC measurements reveal critical deformation events and strain localization.
Calibration against microstructural imaging enables a multiscale finite-element model to represent both average material behavior and localized stress concentrations.
The integrated DIC, imaging, and multiscale FEM approach can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture initiation behavior.
The integrated approach will produce predictions two to three times faster than established simulation methods.
The integrated approach will predict independently measured Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture initiation parameters with errors below 10%.
The hybrid method bypasses computationally intensive full-scale simulations while maintaining predictive accuracy.
Traditional full-scale atomistic or continuum simulations require extensive computational time.
Traditional simulations may inadequately capture rapid localized failure events.
Insufficient DIC resolution may prevent capture of deformation features that control fracture.
Failure to resolve fracture-initiating heterogeneities through microstructural imaging may cause the approach to fail.
Specimen-to-specimen variability may compromise calibration accuracy.
Correlations between real-time strain maps and microstructural features may not generalize across samples with subtle variations in heterogeneity.
Capturing all localized stress concentrations in the integrated FEM remains challenging.
A prediction error greater than 10% relative to independent mechanical-property measurements is predeclared to falsify the hypothesis.
An insignificant statistical correlation between DIC strain maps and imaged microstructural features is predeclared to falsify the hypothesis.
